sections.label: Criminal Procedure Code amendments
sections.summary: The Bill proposes amendments to the Criminal Procedure Code.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The Bill proposes amendments to the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC).

sections.label: SEPP and FME frameworks
sections.summary: The amendments introduce a Sentence for Enhanced Public Protection and a framework for Forensic Medical Examinations.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: First, the new Sentence for Enhanced Public Protection (SEPP) and the second is a new framework for conducting Forensic Medical Examinations (FMEs).

sections.label: New type of sentence
sections.summary: It is a new type of sentence that the Courts can impose.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In essence, it is a new type of sentence, which the Courts can impose.

sections.label: Court specifies minimum term
sections.summary: The Court specifies a term of imprisonment based on the facts, and this is a minimum term.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Court will specify a term of imprisonment for the offender, based on the facts of the case.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But the difference is that this is a minimum term.

sections.label: Custody beyond minimum period
sections.summary: If assessed to pose a risk to others, he can be kept in custody beyond the minimum period when his term ends.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If he is assessed to pose a risk to others, when his term ends, he can be kept in custody beyond the minimum period.

sections.label: Child abuse material offenders
sections.summary: The man had over 100 media discs with child pornography and a thumb drive with 12,000 child abuse images, among other examples of offenders committing egregious acts.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The man also had more than 100 media discs with child pornography and a thumb drive with 12,000 child abuse images.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: There are other examples of such offenders, committing egregious acts.

sections.label: SEPP minimum custody period
sections.summary: The Court specifies a minimum custody period of between five and 20 years when imposing the SEPP.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If the Court imposes the SEPP, it will specify a minimum period of custody.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: That can be anywhere between five and 20 years.

sections.label: Shorter sentences, CT and PD replaced
sections.summary: This can result in the Court imposing shorter sentences upfront, and is intended to replace and streamline the CT and PD regimes.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: This can actually result in the Court imposing shorter sentences upfront.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: This is intended to replace and streamline the current Corrective Training (CT) and Preventive Detention (PD) regimes.

sections.label: SPP fixed term and release
sections.summary: SPP is a fixed term of five to 20 years, with offenders eligible for release on licence after serving two-thirds.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: SPP is for a fixed term of between five and 20 years, and offenders will be eligible for release on licence after serving two-thirds of the sentence.

sections.label: FMEs for accused persons and victims
sections.summary: Police can require accused persons to undergo FMEs without consent, using reasonable force except for intimate body parts or invasive procedures, and refusal is an offence without reasonable excuse; victims generally must consent.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: For accused persons, Police can require them to undergo FMEs, even if they do not consent.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Reasonable force can be used if the FME does not relate to intimate body parts or invasive procedures.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But it will be an offence for an accused person to refuse an FME, unless he has a reasonable excuse, for example, if he has haemophilia and giving a blood sample could endanger his life.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In the case of victims, consent is generally required for FMEs.

sections.label: Inspector rank for intimate FMEs
sections.summary: Only Police officers of the rank of Inspector and above can require an FME involving intimate body parts.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Only Police officers holding the rank of Inspector and above can require an FME involving intimate body parts.

sections.label: FMEs, SEPP, disclosure amendments
sections.summary: Three changes are set out: a legal framework for FMEs, a new Sentence for Enhanced Public Protection, and amendments to the criminal case disclosure regime.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: First, we will establish a legal framework for conducting Forensic Medical Examinations (FMEs); second, we will introduce a new Sentence for Enhanced Public Protection (SEPP); and third, we will make amendments to the disclosure regime for our criminal cases.

sections.label: Safeguards for forensic medical examinations
sections.summary: Establishes safeguards for FMEs, including qualified professionals, Inspector-rank orders, and privacy measures for intimate parts.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: First, we will establish safeguards to ensure that FMEs are conducted safely and sensitively.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: This includes ensuring that only qualified medical professionals conduct examinations and procedures; the person conducting the FME must be satisfied that it will not endanger the subject; the order to perform FME is given by police officers with the rank of Inspector and above; and measures to protect privacy are taken for FMEs involving intimate parts, for example, ensuring that such FMEs that need to be conducted on a female is carried out by a female police officer or a female forensic expert.

sections.label: SEPP changes sentencing landscape
sections.summary: States that SEPP represents a significant change to the sentencing landscape.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: SEPP represents a significant change to our sentencing landscape.

sections.label: Government protection from dangerous offenders
sections.summary: The Government has looked at ways to protect the public from dangerous offenders, with stringent requirements before SEPP.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: Arising from such cases, the Government has been looking at ways to better protect the public from such dangerous offenders.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: There are stringent requirements that must be fulfilled before the court can impose SEPP.

sections.label: SEPP minimum custody and release
sections.summary: Sets a minimum custody period of 5 to 20 years, with release only if the Minister assesses suitability on Board advice.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: When imposing SEPP, the Court will specify a minimum period of custody between 5 and 20 years.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: Offenders will remain in prison for the duration of this minimum period, which cannot be shortened.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: At the end of the minimum period, the offender will be re-evaluated and only released if assessed to be suitable for release by the Minister for Home Affairs, on the advice of a Detention Review Board.

sections.label: Minister reviews non-release decision
sections.summary: If the Minister decides not to release the offender, the Minister must review the decision within a year.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: If the Minister decides not to release the offender, the Minister must review the decision within a year.

sections.label: Warrantless police search power
sections.summary: Clause 5 allows Police to search without warrant where they believe relevant evidence is held by a suspect of an arrestable offence.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: Clause 5 allows the Police to conduct a search without warrant at a place when they have reason to believe that the relevant evidence is in the possession or power of a suspect of an arrestable offence.

sections.label: CNB, immigration, prison arrest powers
sections.summary: Clause 11 empowers CNB, immigration and prison officers to pursue and arrest persons who escaped their agency's lawful custody.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: Clause 11 empowers the Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) officers, immigration officers and prison officers to pursue and arrest a person who has escaped from the lawful custody of their respective agency, another specified LEA, or a prescribed LEA.

sections.label: Kadar disclosure obligations explained
sections.summary: Courts held the Prosecution must disclose additional material beyond the CCD regime, including unused material under the Kadar disclosure obligations.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: The Courts have held that the Prosecution is also obliged to disclose certain additional material on top of what the CCD regime requires.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: I will briefly explain these: first, under the Kadar disclosure obligations (KDO), the Prosecution must disclose unused material that tends to undermine the Prosecution's case or strengthen the Defence's case, and is likely to be either admissible and that might reasonably be regarded as credible and relevant to the guilt or innocence of the accused; or inadmissible, but would provide a real, not fanciful chance of pursuing a line of inquiry that leads to material that is likely to be admissible, and that might reasonably be regarded as credible and relevant to the guilt or innocence of the accused.

sections.label: Statutory footing for disclosure rules
sections.summary: It is desirable to place the common law disclosure rules on a statutory footing for clarity, certainty and coherence.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: One thing was clear to us – it is desirable to place the common law disclosure rules on a statutory footing, for greater clarity, certainty and coherence.

sections.label: Clauses 23 and 42 codify disclosure
sections.summary: Clauses 23 and 42 place the common law disclosure rules on a statutory footing by codifying, clarifying or modifying aspects of the common law.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: First, clauses 23 and 42, place the common law disclosure rules on a statutory footing, by codifying, clarifying or modifying aspects of the common law.

sections.label: ADO after defence commitment
sections.summary: Some common law aspects will be modified or clarified so ADO is given after the accused commits to a defence.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: Some aspects of the common law will be modified or clarified to better align with the sequential nature of the statutory disclosure regime.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: We will provide that ADO is to be given after the accused has committed to a defence, either in his Case for the Defence (CFD) or his testimony, in cases where there is no CFD.

sections.label: Disclosure of unused accused statements
sections.summary: Rules provide that unused accused statements are outside KDO's scope and, in certain cases, disclosed only after testimony or election not to testify.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: Next, we will also provide rules for the disclosure of unused accused statements, specifically, that (a) unused accused statements are outside the scope of KDO; and (b) in non-CCD cases or CCD cases where the CFD is not filed, unused accused statements relevant to the charge are required to be disclosed only after the accused has testified or elected not to testify.

sections.label: Expanding CCD regime
sections.summary: The CCD regime will be further expanded to require compulsory participation in State Court and High Court CCD cases.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: In 2018, we expanded the regime, so that more cases could benefit from pre-trial disclosure.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: We will now further expand the CCD regime to require compulsory participation in both State Court and High Court CCD cases.

sections.label: CFDs in criminal cases
sections.summary: CFDs are regularly filed for most State Court CCD trials, and requiring them avoids delays; changes align High Court with State Court.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: Today, CFDs are regularly filed for most State Court CCD trials and this has contributed to a more efficient criminal justice system.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: Requiring the Defence to file a CFD also avoids potential delays that may arise from the belated disclosure of the Defence's case, which may arise due to a need for further investigations to verify the accused's claims or having to recall witnesses.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: The proposed changes will align the position in High Court cases with that for State Court cases.

sections.label: Prosecution summary of facts
sections.summary: The Prosecution will be required to file a summary of facts in High Court CCD cases, similar to State Court cases.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: For example, we will enhance consistency between the Prosecution's CCD obligations in State Courts cases and High Court cases, by requiring the Prosecution to file a summary of facts in support of the charge in High Court CCD cases, similar to the State Court cases.

sections.label: Personal bond for minor offences
sections.summary: Clause 16 allows release on personal bond for non-bailable offences punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment, as an alternative to bail.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
sentences.text: Clause 16 proposes to allow the Court to release persons accused of relatively minor non-bailable offences – that is, offences punishable with up to seven years’ imprisonment – on personal bond, as an alternative to bail.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
sentences.text: Currently, such accused persons can only be released on bail and, will be remanded if they are offered bail but cannot find a bailor.

sections.label: Prosecution consent and court discretion
sections.summary: The Prosecution must consent before release on personal bond, and the Court can still decide not to release the person.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
sentences.text: For example, the Prosecution must consent, before the person can be released on personal bond.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
sentences.text: Even if the Prosecution consents, the Court can decide not to release the person on personal bail, if it considers that this would not be appropriate.

sections.label: Victim consent timeframe
sections.summary: The question asks the Minister to clarify when Police determine a victim cannot provide consent within a reasonable time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Can the Minister clarify what are the circumstances when the Police will determine that a victim is unable to provide consent within a reasonable time?

sections.label: Codifying Common Law disclosure obligations
sections.summary: The amendments codify Common Law obligations so relevant evidence in the prosecution's possession is available to the defence pre-trial and adduced at trial.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: I welcome the amendments to codify the Common Law obligations into legislation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: These amendments address a fundamental concern of ensuring that relevant and material evidence in the prosecutions' possession, which either incriminates or exculpates the accused, is made available to the defence at the pre-trial stage and is subsequently adduced at trial so that the Court is apprised of the full facts and all available evidence.

sections.label: Continuing prosecution disclosure and SEPP
sections.summary: New section 221d makes the prosecution's obligation to serve certain materials continuing, but does not require disclosure of prosecution witness statements; SEPP offenders are not automatically released.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: In this regard, I welcome the new section 221d which makes it clear that the prosecution has a continuing obligation to serve certain materials on the defence if the prosecution becomes aware of such materials before the accused is convicted or acquitted.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: However, the present amendments made it clear that the ADO does not require disclosure of prosecution witness statements.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: With the SEPP, an offender will not be automatically released after serving the minimum sentence unless he or she is assessed to no longer post a threat to the public.

sections.label: Personal bond eligibility
sections.summary: Accused persons facing charges with a maximum imprisonment of not more than seven years are eligible for release on personal bond.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Accused persons will be eligible to be released on personal bond if they are facing charges where the maximum imprisonment for the offence is not more than seven years.

sections.label: Reasons for no compensation
sections.summary: If the court decides not to award compensation, it has to give its reasons for not doing so.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: One change will be that if the court decides not to award compensation, it has to give its reasons for not doing so.

sections.label: SEPP release review and first-time offenders
sections.summary: Release from a minimum custody period of five to 20 years is subject to annual Ministry review, and under proposed section 304B an SEPP sentence could be imposed on a first-time offender with no prior records.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The concern largely stems from the fact that even though the offender has been sentenced by the court to a minimum custody period of between five to 20 years, when precisely the offender will be released is subject to annual review by the Ministry; in fact, he may never be released if deemed to be still dangerous.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Under the proposed section 304B of the Code, an SEPP sentence could be imposed even on someone who is appearing before the Courts for the first time, with no prior criminal records.

sections.label: False positives in dangerousness predictions
sections.summary: Predictions of dangerousness can be wrong, and US research literature shows that out of every three persons predicted to commit future violence, only one will do so.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Predictions of dangerousness, even by trained professionals, can be wrong.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: There is ample research literature in the United States (US) that predictions of future violence, more often than not, turn out cases which are "false positives" and that out of every three persons predicted to commit future violence, only one will do so.

sections.label: SEPP over-detention risk
sections.summary: The SEPP amplifies the risk of over-detention because there is no definite release date.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In the case of the SEPP, the risk of over-detention is amplified because there is no definite release date.

sections.label: Long sentences in SEPP scenarios
sections.summary: Two offenders deemed possibly suitable for the SEPP received 40-year and 45-year terms from consecutive jail terms for sexual offences against multiple victims.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In two of the scenarios highlighted that were deemed possibly suitable for the SEPP, the offenders were sentenced by the Court to very long imprisonment terms of 40 years and 45 years for sexual offences against multiple victims.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: These very long jail terms were the result of the jail terms imposed for several charges being ordered by the Court to run consecutively, that is, some jail terms were added up, to run one after another.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I pause here to note that 40-plus years is a much longer period of time than the currently proposed minimum detention period for the SEPP of five to 20 years.

sections.label: Release assessment methods questioned
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Ministries of Law and Home Affairs for greater detail on assessment methods and whether additional measures are considered for sexual offenders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: While I am assured to learn that the assessment of an offender’s suitability for release takes into consideration many factors, including the results of psychological tests, would the Ministries of Law and Home Affairs share in greater detail, what methods are used in these assessments to determine if the convicts will pose a threat to the public?

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Regarding sexual offenders deemed suitable for release, especially those who had attacked children, would the Ministries consider additional measures for public safety?

sections.label: Supplementary measures for offenders
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether the Ministries considered including the options as supplementary measures and what their views are.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Have the Ministries looked into and considered whether these options may be included as supplementary measures for such offenders in Singapore?

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: What are the Ministries’ views on these measures?

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The suggested changes will strengthen our existing legal frameworks, improve law and order, and make it easier to identify, arrest, charge, and detain those committing serious crimes.

sections.label: Sexual Crime and Family Violence Command
sections.summary: In 2023 the Singapore Police Force established the Sexual Crime and Family Violence Command to strengthen investigative capabilities, victim care and collaborations.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: First, I understand that in 2023, the Singapore Police Force (SPF) established the Sexual Crime and Family Violence Command, which aims to strengthen investigative capabilities, improve victim care processes in sexual crime and family violence cases, and foster closer collaborations with other public agencies.

sections.label: Support for unreported sexual abuse
sections.summary: The speaker asks what support is available for victims of sexual abuse who have chosen not to report to the Police.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Related to this, I would like to know what support is available for victims of sexual abuse who have chosen not to report their concerns to the Police.

sections.label: SEPP prisoners housing and support
sections.summary: The speaker suggests dedicated housing, multidisciplinary support, independent visitor oversight, halfway house placement, independent advocates and restorative justice for SEPP prisoners.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Given the unique needs of this group of prisoners and their potential long-term or permanent incarceration, I suggest that they be accommodated within dedicated housing units separate from other prisoners, and that they receive specialised and multidisciplinary support to enhance their rehabilitation.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Additionally, it is important that prisoners on SEPP are subject to oversight by independent visitors who are authorised to meet with prisoners to assess the level of care they are receiving and whether they have any concerns or complaints.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I understand that a similar scheme is already in place in the form of Board of Visitors for Community Rehabilitation Centres and Drug Rehabilitation Centres, and perhaps this scheme could be extended to include those facilities that will house prisoners on SEPP.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: My question is whether there are provisions for such prisoners to be placed within a specialised halfway house to support them with their reintegration process.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Additionally, is it feasible for the committee that considers applications for release on licence to include independent advocates to represent the best interests of the prisoner.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I would also like to suggest implementing the principles and practices of restorative justice to increase the understanding of victim impact and offer greater community support for prisoners who are willing to participate in a restorative process.

sections.label: FMEs and dangerous offender detention
sections.summary: The major measures include a new legislative framework for FMEs and power to further detain dangerous and high-risk offenders who threaten the public.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: The major measures include establishing a new legislative framework for FMEs and granting the power to further detain dangerous and high-risk offenders who pose a threat to the public.

sections.label: Appropriate Adult Scheme update sought
sections.summary: The speaker seeks an update on the Appropriate Adult Scheme's status, including volunteer numbers, profiles, training, accomplishments, challenges and future plans.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: A number of the AAs who are volunteers are generalists trained probably once only upon recruitment and they play a limited role in safeguarding the rights and well-being of vulnerable persons.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: I, therefore, seek an update from the Ministry on the Appropriate Adult Scheme's current status, including the number of volunteers deployed, their profiles, the training provided, accomplishments, challenges and some future plans for advancement of this important scheme.

sections.label: Measures for vulnerable individuals
sections.summary: The speaker seeks the Ministry's responses on specialised interview techniques, enhancing the Appropriate Adults Scheme, more trained personnel and better interagency coordination.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: In summary, I would to seek, therefore, the Ministry's considered responses to better adoption of the measures that I have mentioned to safeguard the interests of vulnerable individuals in our criminal justice system: (a) the use of specialised interview techniques; (b) enhancing the Appropriate Adults Scheme for a safe and supportive interview setting; (c) more trained personnel in LEAs, including the Public Defence Office; and (d) better interagency coordination and collaborations for better outcomes.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Failing to do so would constitute an injustice.

sections.label: SPP and SEPP replace CT and PD
sections.summary: The SPP and the more severe SEPP framework replace the existing Corrective Training and Preventive Detention regimes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The SPP and the more severe SEPP framework replace the existing Corrective Training (CT) and Preventive Detention (PD) regimes.

sections.label: CT and PD regimes
sections.summary: The CT regime applies to offenders aged 18 and above for five to 14 years, and the PD regime to offenders aged 30 and above for seven to 20 years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The CT regime applies to offenders aged 18 years and above, with a term of between five and 14 years; and the PD regime applies to offenders aged 30 years and above, with a more substantial term of between seven and 20 years, as it is intended to apply to more serious offenders.

sections.label: SEPP minimum sentence and Minister
sections.summary: The Court pronounces a minimum sentence under the SEPP, but the Minister, advised by a panel of experts, may extend incarceration indefinitely.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: While the Court would pronounce a minimum sentence when sentencing the offender to the SEPP, the actual period of incarceration may be extended indefinitely by the Minister, who will be advised, of course, by a panel of experts.

sections.label: Minister release or continued detention
sections.summary: Under the SEPP, the Minister may release the offender on license after the minimum term or continue detention up to life, after expert advice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Under the SEPP, the Minister may release the offender on license after he has served the minimum term or he may decide to continue to detain the offender up to life, of course, after having taken advice from a panel of experts.

sections.label: SEPP and sentencing power abdication
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether the SEPP abdicates the Court's sentencing powers to the executive and asks what standard of proof the Minister applies.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I acknowledge that the SEPP is, in and of itself, a sentence, that is a Court would have to sentence an offender to be subject to the SEPP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: But does this come close to an abdication of the sentencing powers of the Court at the end of the minimum period of the sentence to the executive?

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In this regard, the principle of the Court's role in sentencing articulated by the hon the Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon in his keynote address at the Sentencing Conference in October 2022 is instructive and I quote his honour: "...although Parliament may determine the scope of the courts' sentencing power through the legislative scheme that it prescribes, including by specifying mandatory or minimum sentences, the sentencing function of the courts cannot be enlisted to disguise what in substance is a decision of the Executive." In this regard, a salient clarification is what standard of proof would the Minister apply when considering the report of the Detention Review Board?

sections.label: Warrantless police search powers
sections.summary: The Bill empowers Police to conduct warrantless searches of suspects' premises and workplaces, and the speaker asks when warrants would still be needed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Once the Bill is passed, the Police will now be empowered to conduct searches without warrants when they have reason to believe that the relevant evidence that may aid in their investigations is in the possession of or power of within the power of a suspect of an arrestable offence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: They may search the premises of another person if the suspect is at that second person's premises and they may even check the workplaces of the suspect.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: These are very wide powers for searches to be conducted without sanction by the courts via a warrant.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: First, following the passing of this Bill, in what circumstances would the Police now have to obtain a warrant from the courts before carrying out a search?

sections.label: Force for FMEs and warrants
sections.summary: The speaker asks about section 40I allowing reasonable force for FMEs, when a person is a suspect, internal approval, and whether a warrant safeguard was considered.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This will help the Police obtain evidence that is often determinative in a case.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I am, however, concerned about the new section 40I which will allow Police officers to use reasonable force to carry out FMEs which, based on the press release by the Ministry, could be used to obtain, amongst other things, hair samples and buccal or cheek swaps.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Could the Minister elaborate on when a person would be considered a "suspect", whether internal approval would have to be sought by investigating officers before resorting to force and what exactly may force be used to obtain?

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I would also like to ask whether the Minister had considered including a provision to require that the Police first obtain a warrant from the courts before using force and why such an institutional safeguard was not included.

sections.label: Withholding intimate documentary exhibits
sections.summary: Under the Bill, prosecution need not serve documentary exhibits showing genital or anal regions or a woman's breasts on the Defence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Under the Bill, where a documentary exhibit in a case for the prosecution includes an image of an individual's genital or anal region, or a woman's breasts, the prosecution is not required to serve the exhibit on the Defence.

sections.label: Prosecution serving witness statements
sections.summary: New section 221B(1) requires the Prosecution to serve on the defence the statement of any material witness relating to the charges.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Additionally, the new section 221B(1) requires the Prosecution to serve on the defence the statement of any material witness that relates to the charges.

sections.label: Remand period limits and numbers
sections.summary: Period lengths are capped at one month for SPP and two months for SEPP, but the number of periods is not constrained, risking indefinite remand.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The maximum length of each period is clearly circumscribed – one month for SPP and two months for SEPP – to enshrine some fairness in the process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: But the number of periods does not seem constrained by the same safeguard.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: This opens the possibility that an offender gets remanded indefinitely while the entity preparing the report – the Commissioner of Prisoners for SPP and the psychiatrist for SEPP – fails to submit it in a timely fashion.

sections.label: Sexual assault reports in Singapore
sections.summary: Sexual crimes remain a key concern, with close to 10,000 reports between 2019 and 2022 and a 61% rise in family-member cases involving victims below 16.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Of the many faces that criminality can take, sexual crimes remain a key concern in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: There are close to 10,000 reports of sexual assault between 2019 and 2022.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: The number of sexual assault cases involving victims below 16 years old allegedly committed by family members increased by 61% in 2019 to 2022.

sections.label: SPP and SEPP target offenders
sections.summary: The new SPP and SEPP aim to tackle offenders whose imprisonment would have spared more innocent lives from lifelong trauma of sexual abuse.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Had such perpetrators remained behind bars, more innocent lives would have been spared from the lifelong trauma of sexual abuse.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: These are exactly the type of offenders that the new SPP and the SEPP aims to tackle.

sections.label: Courts tailor sentences for protection
sections.summary: Amendments give Courts, not the Government, levers to tailor sentences for public protection, with SEPP limited to serious offences and courts considering risk assessment reports.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: These amendments will provide the Courts, and not the Government, with the necessary levers to tailor sentences based on the severity of offences, for public protection.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: It is notable that the SEPP is limited to serious offences, such as culpable homicide, rape, sexual offences involving vulnerable persons such as persons with mental disabilities and minors; and the courts may consider reports, that is, risk assessment reports by appointed professionals.

sections.label: Police warrantless search powers
sections.summary: Proposed amendments empower police to search without a warrant for evidence held by suspects of arrestable offences, and enhance non-police agencies' powers for predicate offences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Under the proposed amendments, the police will be empowered to conduct searches without a warrant when they have reason to believe that the relevant evidence is in the possession or power of a suspect of an arrestable offence, allowing searches of arrested persons at the point of arrest for safety reasons.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: In this regard, could the Ministry clarify how it will ensure the judicious use of these enhanced powers by the police to prevent overreach and protect the rights of individuals?

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: What are the review and training mechanisms in place to guide officers?

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: It is also proposed for the powers of non-police law enforcement agencies to be enhanced to deal with matters arising from predicate offences under their purview.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: This is especially important in ensuring that the suitable law enforcement agency deals with the matters they are most familiar with, which is important to maximise operational efficiency considering Singapore’s size.

sections.label: Consent standards for medical evaluation
sections.summary: Proposed section 40H sets consent standards for medical evaluation across three age groups of alleged victims.

sentences.speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Under the proposed section 40H, there is a distinction for standards of consent for medical evaluation drawn over three groups of alleged victims: (a) alleged victims below 14 years old requiring the consent of a parent or guardian; (b) alleged victims between 14 and 16 years old requiring the consent of a parent or guardian and that of the alleged victim; and (c) alleged victims above 16 years old requiring only the consent of the alleged victim.

sections.label: Refusal and reasonable force
sections.summary: Sections 40I to K cover refusal of FME and use of reasonable force in certain cases.

sentences.speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Thirdly, Mr Deputy Speaker, under sections 40I to K, regarding refusal for FME and use of reasonable force in certain cases, I agree that refusal for FME could constitute an offence and can appreciate the need for reasonable force to retrieve samples or conduct FME for certain cases.

sections.label: Body samples and invasive blood
sections.summary: Section 40E lists body samples, with only blood explicitly considered an invasive sample.

sentences.speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In section 40E, these are all articulated as body samples, but only the sample of blood is explicitly considered as an invasive sample.

sections.label: Clarifying samples under reasonable force
sections.summary: It would help to clarify which samples are permitted with reasonable force on a non-consenting person and considered non-invasive.

sentences.speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Given that the type of samples permitted for a consenting FME are already articulated in section 40E, for clarity, it would be helpful to clarify what samples are permitted with use of reasonable force on a non-consenting person and also considered non-invasive.

sections.label: Principles behind Seventh Schedule offences
sections.summary: The Minister is asked to explain the principles behind the selected offences in the Seventh Schedule under SEPP.

sentences.speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: First, could the Minister explain the principles behind the selected offences in the Seventh Schedule under SEPP?

sections.label: SPP and SEPP clarifications
sections.summary: Clarification is sought on the intended gain of SPP and SEPP, its measurement, and the number of offenders affected.

sentences.speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Second, I would like to gain clarification over what is envisioned as the intended gain of SPP and SEPP, and how will this eventually be measured?

sentences.speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Third, what are the numbers of current and ex-offenders this Bill could impact and how many of them could qualify for SPP and/or SEPP at their next offence?

sections.label: Reservations on SEPP sentencing powers
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether existing approaches could be improved instead of introducing SPP and/or SEPP, and states reservations about SEPP's gains, proportionality and encroachment on civil liberties.

sentences.speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Would it be possible then to focus on doing this better instead of introducing SPP and/or SEPP?

sentences.speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I do have reservations relating to SEPP specifically, its achievable gains and proportionality in the sentencing framework, as well as its encroachment into civil liberties, even if it is reserved for the most heinous and predatory among us.

sections.label: US stop and frisk comparison
sections.summary: The speaker notes the Senior Parliamentary Secretary's clarification that the powers do not amount to US stop and frisk, citing NYPD 2022 figures of 15,102 stops and 9,750 not arrested or summonsed.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: While I appreciate Senior Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam's clarification in her speech that the powers do not amount to stop and frisk in the US, where according to the New York Police Department (NYPD)'s annual reports, in 2022, 15,102 stops were recorded, but 9,750 were eventually not arrested or given a summons, at 65%.

sections.label: Inspector rank for intimate inspections
sections.summary: The Bill's framework for FME specifies that only Police officers holding at least the rank of Inspector may require inspections involving intimate parts.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: In this same Bill, the proposed legislative framework for FME specifies that only Police officers holding at least the rank of Inspector have the power to require inspections involving intimate parts.

sections.label: Obstructing lawful search arrestable
sections.summary: Under the Bill, obstructing a Police officer from a lawful search becomes an arrestable offence.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Under the Bill, obstructing a Police officer from a lawful search becomes an arrestable offence.

sections.label: Sentences for sexual offenders seen as low
sections.summary: Despite enhanced sentences for certain sexual crimes from March 2022, many feel sentences for sexual offenders are too low and do little to deter similar acts.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Even so, and despite enhanced sentences for certain sexual crimes taking effect from March 2022, many feel that sentences meted out to sexual offenders are too low and do not do much to deter others from committing similar acts.

sections.label: Lim Chun Wing FME evidence case
sections.summary: In Lim Chun Wing vs Public Prosecutor, Lim broke in, assaulted and raped the victim, was arrested the same day, and FME revealed the victim's DNA on his genitals; the amendment applies to accused and victims with different treatment.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Conversely, in the case of Lim Chun Wing vs Public Prosecutor, Lim broke into the victim's house, assaulted and raped her before fleeing.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: He was arrested on the same day and FME conducted on him revealed the victim's DNA on his genitals.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: While we acknowledge the critical role of FMEs in obtaining forensic evidence, it is important to note that the amendment applies to both accused and victims, although there is different treatment.

sections.label: Minor victim consent preference
sections.summary: Asks whether a minor sexual crime victim may have a different preference for taking samples and evidence than their parents, and how consent is handled.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Are there potential incidents where a minor who is a victim of a sexual crime may have a different preference for the taking of such samples and evidence, as compared to their parents, and how will the issue of consent be handled then?

sections.label: Victim care provisions
sections.summary: States the process can be challenging for such victims and the public should know provisions like separate rooms and female Police officers.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: The process can be challenging for such victims and it is in the public's interest to know what the provisions are, such as separate rooms, for example, which have been designed with victim care in mind and the involvement of female Police officers exclusively.

sections.label: Consent for FME
sections.summary: States that under proposed section 40H of the CPC, a Police officer may not require an alleged victim to undergo an FME without consent.

sentences.speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Under the proposed new section 40H of the CPC, it is, quite correctly, very clearly stated that a Police officer may not require an alleged victim to undergo an FME, unless the victim consents to the examination.

sections.label: Consent from deputy or donee
sections.summary: States that if an alleged victim cannot consent in time due to a physical or mental condition causing evidence loss, Police may seek consent from a deputy or donee.

sentences.speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Notwithstanding the requirements for the grant of express consent, if the alleged victim is unable to provide consent within a reasonable time due to a physical or mental condition and that delay results in loss, contamination or degradation of the required evidence, the Police are permitted under the new law to seek consent instead from a deputy or donee, on behalf of the alleged victim.

sections.label: FME by woman
sections.summary: Asks whether proposed section 40G, requiring FMEs on intimate regions of a woman to be by a woman, covers a male officer examining a legally male person identifying as female.

sentences.speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: My final clarification on the new FME provisions relates to the proposed section 40G of CPC, which specifies that FMEs involving intimate regions of the body may only be carried out by a woman, if the subject of the examination is also a woman.

sentences.speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: For example, will the new rules allow a male Police officer or forensic specialist to conduct an FME on a person who is legally male, but identifies as female and has yet to undergo gender confirmation surgery or change their registered sex officially?

sections.label: SEPP policy rationale
sections.summary: States the primary policy rationale for SEPP is to protect the public from dangerous offenders committing serious violent and serious sexual offences.

sentences.speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The primary stated policy rationale for SEPP is to protect the public from specific types of dangerous offenders, namely, from those who commit serious violent offences, such as culpable homicide and attempted murder, as well as serious sexual offences, such as rape and the sexual penetration of a minor.

sections.label: SEPP psychiatrist report and detention
sections.summary: Courts must consider a psychiatrist's report and offender's report before an SEPP, which detains offenders for five to 20 years.

sentences.speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Before imposing the sentence, the new proposed law requires the Courts to call for and consider a psychiatrist's report as well as any report submitted by the offender or their lawyer on the offender's risk of causing serious physical or sexual harm to others.

sentences.speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: That being said, under an SEPP, an offender will be detained for a minimum term of between five and 20 years.

sections.label: Indeterminate detention if unsuitable
sections.summary: An offender found unsuitable for release may be detained for an indeterminate period.

sentences.speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: If the offender is found to be unsuitable for release, they may continue to be detained for an indeterminate period of time.

sections.label: Assurance on victim-centric solutions
sections.summary: The Member seeks the Minister's assurance that victim-centric and trauma-informed solutions continue and expand despite enhanced SEPP penalties.

sentences.speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As a final point, I seek the Minister's assurance that even if enhanced penalties are introduced under SEPP, that the Government will continue to implement and expand victim-centric and trauma-informed solutions, especially in cases where violence is committed against women.

sections.label: Clause 11 cross-department arrest powers
sections.summary: Clause 11 empowers CNB, ICA and Prisons officers to pursue and re-arrest persons escaping other Home Team Departments' custody.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Clause 11 of the Bill empowers officers of CNB, ICA and the Singapore Prison Service (Prisons) to pursue and re-arrest persons escaping from the lawful custody of other Home Team Departments (HTDs), including the Police.

sections.label: Forensic medical evidence powers question
sections.summary: The Member asks the number and status of cases where lack of legal powers for forensic medical evidence impeded investigations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The proposed Division 5 of clause 7, which formally empowers the Police and other specialists to obtain forensic medical evidence critical for investigations, with the closure of this legislative gap and the improved potential for solving crimes, can the Minister share the number and status of cases in the past five years, in which the current lack of legal powers for FME has impeded investigations?

sections.label: SPP and SEPP prevent automatic release
sections.summary: The severity of the proposed SPP and SEPP conveys the desire to prevent dangerous offenders' automatic release after their jail term.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Next, on the new sentences for public protection, the severity of the proposed SPP and SEPP conveys our desire to prevent dangerous offenders from being automatically released from prison after the end of their jail term.

sections.label: Court process personal bond release
sections.summary: Clauses 12 and 13 let Courts and Police release accused persons on personal bond for offences punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: On the improvements in Court processes, clauses 12 and 13 provide for the Courts and the Police to release accused persons on personal bond for offences punishable with imprisonment of up to seven years.

sections.label: SEPP for dangerous offenders
sections.summary: SEPP detains dangerous or repeat offenders of serious hurt and sexual offences until assessed as no longer a threat, with reviews.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Under this proposal, known as SEPP in short, which we are finally able to debate on today, dangerous offenders or repeat offenders who commit very serious hurt and sexual offences will not be automatically released after serving their sentence, but would be released only after having been assessed as no longer posing a threat to the public.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: SEPP is not an alternative to life sentencing.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Under SEPP, I see that Judges are making their decisions aided by expert risk assessment reports by professionals from the Institute of Mental Health (IMH) or others and there is a review built in at their end of their original sentence where assessments are conducted by expert psychiatrists and a detention review board.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: This review is also triggered after every two years to provide a chance for the offenders to be considered for release.

sections.label: Support for SEPP Bill
sections.summary: The speaker supports introducing SEPP through the Bill to better protect the public from dangerous, repeated offenders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: We therefore cannot afford to turn a blind eye to this alarming issue.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Hence, I am in support of the introduction of SEPP through the Bill as it seeks to better protect the public from dangerous, repeated offenders.

sections.label: SEPP application point question
sections.summary: The passage asks whether SEPP is applied at the point of sentencing or at the point of release.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Is it applied at the point of sentencing or at the point of release?

sections.label: Number of SEPP offenders
sections.summary: The passage asks how many current offenders serving sentence could be placed on SEPP with indefinite detention possible.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Based on the current offenders serving their sentence, what will be the number of offenders that could be placed on SEPP for which indefinite detention could be a possibility?

sections.label: No extension to non-Home Team LEAs
sections.summary: The passage states there are currently no plans to extend the powers to non-Home Team law enforcement agencies.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: Currently, we do not have plans to extend the powers to non-Home Team LEAs.
